Medicine-06.question: ১) ECG finding in thyrotoxicosis
Medicine-06.exp:
Sinus tachycardia is the most common ECG finding in thyrotoxicosis. Excess T3 increases β₁-adrenergic receptor sensitivity and sympathetic activity, resulting in increased heart rate, myocardial contractility, and cardiac output. In older patients, atrial fibrillation is the most common clinically significant arrhythmia.

  • ক) Sinus bradycardia → Seen in hypothyroidism, not thyrotoxicosis.

  • গ) Low voltage ECG → Characteristic of myxedema (hypothyroidism), pericardial effusion, obesity, or COPD.

  • ঘ) Wide QRS → Suggests bundle branch block, ventricular rhythm, hyperkalemia, or drug toxicity; not a typical finding in thyrotoxicosis.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

Topic: ECG in Thyrotoxicosis

High-Yield Points:

  • Definition: Clinical syndrome due to excess circulating thyroid hormones.

  • Pathophysiology: T3 increases β₁-receptor sensitivity, causing a hyperdynamic cardiovascular state.

  • Clinical Features: Tachycardia, palpitations, tremor, weight loss, heat intolerance.

  • Diagnosis: ↓ TSH, ↑ Free T4/T3.

  • Investigation of Choice (IOC): Thyroid Function Test (TSH + Free T4).

  • Gold Standard (GS): No single gold standard; diagnosis is based on thyroid function tests.

  • Important Associations: Atrial fibrillation, high-output heart failure, Graves' disease.

  • Common MCQ Trap: Sinus tachycardia is the most common ECG finding, whereas atrial fibrillation is the most common clinically significant arrhythmia (especially in the elderly).

  • Mnemonic: "Hyperthyroid = Hyper Heart."

Exam Pearl

The commonest ECG finding in thyrotoxicosis is sinus tachycardia; in elderly patients, always think of atrial fibrillation.

Medicine-06.question: ২) 1st line therapy in non obese patient with DM
Medicine-06.exp:
Metformin is the first-line drug for Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM) in both obese and non-obese patients, unless contraindicated (e.g., severe renal impairment). It improves insulin sensitivity, decreases hepatic gluconeogenesis, and increases peripheral glucose uptake. It is weight-neutral or causes mild weight loss, has a low risk of hypoglycemia, and has proven cardiovascular benefits.

Why correct:

  • Metformin is recommended as the initial pharmacological therapy for newly diagnosed T2DM along with lifestyle modification.

  • Older teaching favored sulfonylureas in non-obese patients, but current guidelines (ADA/EASD, Davidson) recommend Metformin regardless of BMI, if there are no contraindications.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • খ) Sitagliptin: A DPP-4 inhibitor; used as add-on therapy, not first-line in most patients.

  • গ) Vildagliptin: Another DPP-4 inhibitor; not the standard initial drug.

  • ঘ) Gliclazide: A sulfonylurea; can cause hypoglycemia and weight gain, usually used when Metformin is contraindicated or as combination therapy.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • First-line drug in T2DM: Metformin (unless contraindicated).

  • Mechanism: Decreases hepatic glucose production and increases insulin sensitivity.

  • Major advantages: No weight gain, low hypoglycemia risk, cardiovascular benefit.

  • Contraindication: eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m², severe renal failure, severe liver disease, conditions predisposing to lactic acidosis.

  • Common adverse effects: GI upset, diarrhea, vitamin B12 deficiency with long-term use.

  • Common MCQ trap: Current guidelines recommend Metformin as first-line even in non-obese patients. The older concept of using sulfonylureas first in non-obese patients is outdated.

Exam Pearl

For almost all newly diagnosed Type 2 DM patients—whether obese or non-obese— Metformin is the first-line pharmacological therapy unless contraindicated.

Medicine-06.question: ৩) Symptoms of thyrotoxicosis excludes
Medicine-06.exp:
Menorrhagia is not a typical feature of thyrotoxicosis. Excess thyroid hormone causes increased metabolism and enhanced β-adrenergic activity, leading to symptoms such as weight loss, heat intolerance, and palpitations. In females, thyrotoxicosis more commonly causes oligomenorrhea, hypomenorrhea, or amenorrhea due to disruption of the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis.

Why correct:

  • Menorrhagia is more commonly associated with hypothyroidism, not thyrotoxicosis.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • ক) Weight loss: A classic symptom due to increased basal metabolic rate.

  • খ) Heat intolerance: Occurs because of increased heat production.

  • গ) Palpitation: Common due to sinus tachycardia and increased cardiac sensitivity to catecholamines.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Typical symptoms of thyrotoxicosis: Weight loss, heat intolerance, sweating, palpitations, tremor, anxiety, increased appetite.

  • Menstrual changes: Oligomenorrhea, hypomenorrhea, or amenorrhea are common.

  • Hypothyroidism menstrual change: Menorrhagia is the characteristic finding.

  • Common cardiovascular finding: Sinus tachycardia; atrial fibrillation is common in elderly patients.

  • Common MCQ trap: Menorrhagia → Hypothyroidism, Oligomenorrhea/Amenorrhea → Thyrotoxicosis.

Exam Pearl

Remember the contrast: Hyperthyroidism → Oligomenorrhea/Amenorrhea; Hypothyroidism → Menorrhagia.

Medicine-06.question: ৪) Most common malignant thyroid tumor
Medicine-06.exp:
Papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) is the most common malignant thyroid tumor, accounting for approximately 80–85% of all thyroid cancers. It arises from follicular epithelial cells, has an excellent prognosis, and commonly spreads via the lymphatics to the cervical lymph nodes.

Why correct:

  • Papillary carcinoma is the commonest thyroid malignancy.

  • It is associated with previous radiation exposure to the head and neck.

  • Characteristic histological features include Orphan Annie eye nuclei, nuclear grooves, and psammoma bodies.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • খ) Follicular carcinoma: Second most common thyroid malignancy; spreads mainly by hematogenous route to bone and lungs.

  • গ) Medullary carcinoma: Arises from parafollicular (C) cells, secretes calcitonin, and is associated with MEN 2 syndrome.

  • ঘ) Anaplastic tumor: Highly aggressive and has the worst prognosis, but it is rare.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Most common thyroid cancer: Papillary carcinoma (80–85%).

  • Cell of origin: Follicular epithelial cell.

  • Route of spread: Lymphatic spread to cervical lymph nodes.

  • Histology: Orphan Annie eye nuclei, psammoma bodies, nuclear grooves.

  • Risk factor: Childhood head and neck radiation.

  • Most common overall thyroid malignancy: Papillary carcinoma.

  • Common MCQ trap: Papillary → Lymphatic spread; Follicular → Hematogenous spread.

Exam Pearl

"Papillary = Most Common + Lymphatic spread + Psammoma bodies + Orphan Annie eye nuclei."

Medicine-06.question: ৫) Sign of hypothyroidism
Medicine-06.exp:
Weight gain is a characteristic feature of hypothyroidism due to reduced basal metabolic rate (BMR), decreased thermogenesis, and accumulation of mucopolysaccharides causing fluid retention. Patients typically present with weight gain despite poor appetite, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin, and lethargy.

Why correct:

  • Weight gain is a classic manifestation of hypothyroidism.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • খ) Tremor: A feature of hyperthyroidism due to increased β-adrenergic activity.

  • গ) Lid lag: A classical sign of thyrotoxicosis (especially Graves' disease), not hypothyroidism.

  • ঘ) Palmar erythema: Seen in hyperthyroidism, chronic liver disease, and pregnancy; not a feature of hypothyroidism.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Common features of hypothyroidism: Weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation, dry coarse skin, fatigue, bradycardia, delayed relaxation of deep tendon reflexes.

  • Cardiovascular sign: Bradycardia.

  • ECG finding: Sinus bradycardia and low-voltage complexes may be present.

  • Common cause: Hashimoto thyroiditis (iodine-sufficient areas).

  • Diagnosis: ↑ TSH, ↓ Free T4 (primary hypothyroidism).

  • Common MCQ trap: Weight gain = Hypothyroidism; Weight loss, tremor, lid lag, palmar erythema = Hyperthyroidism.

Exam Pearl

Remember the contrast: Hypothyroidism = Weight gain + Bradycardia + Cold intolerance; Hyperthyroidism = Weight loss + Tachycardia + Heat intolerance + Tremor.

Medicine-06.question: ৬) Hormones that antagonise to insulin
Medicine-06.exp:
Growth hormone (GH) is a counter-regulatory hormone that antagonizes the action of insulin. It increases hepatic gluconeogenesis, decreases glucose uptake by peripheral tissues, and promotes lipolysis, thereby increasing blood glucose levels and causing insulin resistance.

Why correct:

  • Growth hormone has an anti-insulin (diabetogenic) effect.

  • Excess GH (e.g., acromegaly) can lead to glucose intolerance or diabetes mellitus.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • ক) Renin: Regulates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS); does not directly antagonize insulin.

  • খ) Erythropoietin: Stimulates red blood cell production; no anti-insulin action.

  • গ) Parathormone (PTH): Regulates calcium and phosphate metabolism; not an insulin antagonist.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Counter-regulatory (anti-insulin) hormones: Growth hormone, glucagon, cortisol, adrenaline (epinephrine).

  • Action of GH: ↑ Gluconeogenesis, ↓ peripheral glucose uptake, ↑ lipolysis.

  • Clinical association: Acromegaly may cause secondary diabetes mellitus.

  • Common MCQ trap: Remember the four major anti-insulin hormones—GH, glucagon, cortisol, and catecholamines.

Exam Pearl

The four major hormones that oppose insulin are: Glucagon, Growth hormone, Cortisol, and Catecholamines (epinephrine).

Medicine-06.question: ৭) Clinical features of autonomic neuropathy excludes
Medicine-06.exp:
Autonomic neuropathy is a common complication of diabetes mellitus, affecting the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems. Typical manifestations include resting (sinus) tachycardia, anhidrosis, postural hypotension, gastroparesis, nocturnal diarrhea, bladder dysfunction, and erectile dysfunction.

Delayed reflexes to light is not a typical feature of diabetic autonomic neuropathy. Although autonomic neuropathy can cause abnormal pupillary function (e.g., small pupil with sluggish reaction), delayed light reflex is classically associated with conditions such as Argyll Robertson pupil or other neurological disorders, making it the exception in this MCQ.

Why correct:

  • Delayed reflexes to light is not a classical clinical feature of diabetic autonomic neuropathy.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • ক) Nocturnal diarrhoea: A well-recognized gastrointestinal manifestation of autonomic neuropathy.

  • গ) Anhidrosis: Common due to sympathetic sudomotor dysfunction.

  • ঘ) Sinus tachycardia: A classic cardiovascular manifestation caused by vagal denervation.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Cardiovascular features: Resting sinus tachycardia, postural hypotension, silent myocardial ischemia.

  • Gastrointestinal features: Gastroparesis, nocturnal diarrhea, constipation.

  • Genitourinary features: Neurogenic bladder, erectile dysfunction.

  • Sudomotor features: Anhidrosis or abnormal sweating.

  • Pupillary changes: Small pupil with sluggish response may occur, but delayed light reflex is not a classical examination finding.

  • Common MCQ trap: Resting tachycardia is a hallmark of diabetic autonomic neuropathy.

Exam Pearl

Think of diabetic autonomic neuropathy as affecting four systems: Heart (tachycardia), Gut (gastroparesis/diarrhea), Bladder (retention), and Sweat glands (anhidrosis).

Medicine-06.question: ৮) Drugs causing hypothyroidism excludes
Medicine-06.exp:
Levodopa does not cause hypothyroidism. Drugs that commonly induce hypothyroidism include Amiodarone, Lithium, and antithyroid drugs such as Methimazole. These drugs either inhibit thyroid hormone synthesis or interfere with thyroid function.

Why correct:

  • Levodopa is used in the treatment of Parkinson's disease and has no significant role in causing hypothyroidism.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • ক) Amiodarone: Contains a high iodine content and may cause both hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism.

  • খ) Methimazole: An antithyroid drug that inhibits thyroid hormone synthesis; excessive dosing can cause hypothyroidism.

  • ঘ) Lithium: Inhibits thyroid hormone release and is a well-known cause of drug-induced hypothyroidism.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Drugs causing hypothyroidism: Lithium, Amiodarone, Methimazole, Carbimazole, Propylthiouracil (PTU), Interferon-α.

  • Amiodarone: Can cause both hypo- and hyperthyroidism.

  • Lithium: Inhibits thyroid hormone release → goiter and hypothyroidism.

  • Methimazole/PTU: Inhibit thyroid hormone synthesis by blocking thyroid peroxidase (PTU also inhibits peripheral T4→T3 conversion).

  • Common MCQ trap: Amiodarone can produce either hypothyroidism or thyrotoxicosis because of its high iodine content.

Exam Pearl

The most commonly tested drugs causing hypothyroidism are Lithium, Amiodarone, and antithyroid drugs (Methimazole/PTU); Levodopa is not one of them.

Medicine-06.question: ৯) Complications of subtotal thyroidectomy
Medicine-06.exp:
Transient hypocalcaemia is one of the most common complications of subtotal (or total) thyroidectomy. It usually occurs due to temporary injury, edema, or devascularization of the parathyroid glands, leading to reduced parathyroid hormone (PTH) secretion and consequent hypocalcaemia.

Why correct:

  • Transient hypocalcaemia is a well-recognized post-thyroidectomy complication and is usually temporary.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • ক) Hepatotoxicity: A complication of antithyroid drugs (e.g., PTU), not thyroid surgery.

  • গ) Agranulocytosis: A serious adverse effect of Methimazole and PTU, not thyroidectomy.

  • ঘ) Hyperthyroidism: Surgery is performed to treat hyperthyroidism; postoperative hyperthyroidism is not a typical complication (hypothyroidism is more likely after extensive thyroid resection).

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Common complications of thyroidectomy: Transient hypocalcaemia, recurrent laryngeal nerve injury, superior laryngeal nerve injury, postoperative hemorrhage/neck hematoma, wound infection, hypothyroidism.

  • Most common complication: Transient hypocalcaemia.

  • Most feared early complication: Postoperative neck hematoma causing airway obstruction.

  • Signs of hypocalcaemia: Perioral numbness, tingling, Chvostek's sign, Trousseau's sign, muscle cramps, tetany.

  • Common MCQ trap: Hypocalcaemia = Thyroid surgery; Agranulocytosis/Hepatotoxicity = Antithyroid drugs.

Exam Pearl

After thyroidectomy, always think of the "2 Ps": Parathyroid injury → Hypocalcaemia and Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury → Hoarseness.

Medicine-06.question: ১০) Contraindications of radio iodine treatment
Medicine-06.exp:
Radioactive iodine (RAI) therapy is used to treat hyperthyroidism, especially Graves' disease and toxic nodular goiter. However, it is contraindicated or relatively contraindicated in patients with active Graves' ophthalmopathy, as RAI may worsen the eye disease. The absolute contraindications are pregnancy and breastfeeding.

Why correct:

  • Active Graves' ophthalmopathy can worsen after RAI therapy due to an increase in thyroid autoimmunity.

  • In such patients, antithyroid drugs or surgery are preferred, or glucocorticoid prophylaxis may be required if RAI is used.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • ক) Patient >40 years: Not a contraindication; RAI is commonly used in older adults.

  • খ) Thyrotoxicosis: This is an indication for RAI, not a contraindication.

  • ঘ) Hypothyroidism: RAI is not indicated in hypothyroidism, but hypothyroidism itself is not considered a contraindication.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Absolute contraindications to RAI: Pregnancy and breastfeeding.

  • Relative contraindication: Active Graves' ophthalmopathy.

  • Indications: Graves' disease, toxic multinodular goiter, toxic adenoma.

  • Common adverse effect: Permanent hypothyroidism.

  • Common MCQ trap: Active Graves' ophthalmopathy is the correct answer when pregnancy/lactation is not among the options.

Exam Pearl

For RAI therapy, always remember: Pregnancy and breastfeeding are absolute contraindications; active Graves' ophthalmopathy is a relative contraindication because RAI can worsen eye disease.

Medicine-06.question: ১১) Weight loss occur in which endocrine diseases
Medicine-06.exp:
Weight loss is a characteristic feature of thyrotoxicosis due to an increased basal metabolic rate (BMR) and enhanced catabolism of fat and muscle, despite a normal or increased appetite.

Why correct:

  • Thyrotoxicosis causes weight loss, heat intolerance, palpitations, tremor, and increased appetite because of excess T3/T4.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • ক) Acromegaly: Usually causes soft tissue overgrowth and organ enlargement, not weight loss.

  • গ) Conn's syndrome: Characterized by hypertension and hypokalemia due to excess aldosterone; weight loss is not a typical feature.

  • ঘ) Cushing's syndrome: Causes weight gain, central obesity, moon face, and buffalo hump due to excess cortisol.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Weight loss endocrine disorders: Thyrotoxicosis, Addison's disease, uncontrolled Type 1 diabetes mellitus.

  • Weight gain endocrine disorders: Hypothyroidism, Cushing's syndrome, insulin therapy.

  • Thyrotoxicosis features: Weight loss, heat intolerance, tremor, palpitations, sweating, increased appetite.

  • Cushing's syndrome features: Central obesity, moon face, buffalo hump, purple striae, hypertension.

  • Conn's syndrome features: Hypertension, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis.

  • Common MCQ trap: Weight loss despite increased appetite is highly suggestive of thyrotoxicosis.

Exam Pearl

The classic endocrine disease causing weight loss with increased appetite is thyrotoxicosis.

Medicine-06.question: ১২) The earliest change in ECG of AMI is
Medicine-06.exp:
The earliest ECG change in Acute Myocardial Infarction (AMI) is ST-segment deviation, usually ST elevation in STEMI due to acute transmural myocardial injury. Although hyperacute (tall, peaked) T waves may appear even earlier, they are not listed among the options. Therefore, ST deviation is the correct answer.

Why correct:

  • ST elevation is the earliest classical ECG finding of acute STEMI.

  • It reflects acute myocardial injury before myocardial necrosis develops.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • ক) T inversion: Occurs later, indicating myocardial ischemia or evolving infarction.

  • গ) Pathological Q wave: Develops hours to days later and indicates myocardial necrosis.

  • ঘ) Widening of QRS: Not a typical early ECG feature of AMI.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Earliest ECG change in AMI: Hyperacute T wave (if included in options).

  • Earliest classical ECG finding: ST-segment elevation.

  • Later changes: T-wave inversion followed by pathological Q waves.

  • Biochemical marker appearing earliest: Cardiac Troponin (high-sensitivity assay).

  • Common MCQ trap: If hyperacute T wave is absent from the options, choose ST elevation (ST deviation).

Exam Pearl

Sequence to remember: Hyperacute T wave → ST elevation → T-wave inversion → Pathological Q wave.

Medicine-06.question: ১৩) Most common clinical signs found in symmetrical sensory polyneuropathy of diabetes ?
Medicine-06.option2: Diminished perception of pain and temperature
Medicine-06.exp:
Distal symmetrical sensory polyneuropathy (DSPN) is the most common form of diabetic neuropathy. It typically affects the longest nerves first, producing a glove-and-stocking pattern of sensory loss. The earliest and most common clinical sign on examination is diminished vibration sense, usually detected with a 128-Hz tuning fork over the great toe.

Why correct:

  • Loss of vibration sense is the most common objective clinical sign of diabetic symmetrical sensory polyneuropathy.

  • It reflects involvement of large myelinated nerve fibers.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • খ) Diminished perception of pain and temperature: Occurs due to small fiber neuropathy, but it is not the most common clinical sign.

  • গ) Burning sensation of the feet: A common symptom, not a clinical sign.

  • ঘ) Extensor plantar response: Indicates upper motor neuron (UMN) involvement and is not a feature of diabetic peripheral neuropathy.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Most common diabetic neuropathy: Distal symmetrical sensorimotor polyneuropathy.

  • Most common symptom: Burning pain or numbness of the feet.

  • Most common clinical sign: Reduced vibration sense.

  • Distribution: Glove-and-stocking pattern.

  • Examination: Test vibration with a 128-Hz tuning fork and protective sensation with a 10-g monofilament.

  • Common MCQ trap: Burning feet = symptom; Loss of vibration = sign.

Exam Pearl

In diabetic peripheral neuropathy, the most common symptom is burning feet, whereas the most common clinical sign is diminished vibration sense.

Medicine-06.question: ১৪) Which investigation will help to differentiate between a Charcot joint and osteomyelitis?
Medicine-06.exp:
MRI is the best imaging modality to differentiate Charcot neuroarthropathy from osteomyelitis in diabetic patients. It has excellent soft tissue and bone marrow resolution, allowing detection of bone marrow edema, cortical destruction, abscess formation, sinus tracts, and soft tissue infection, which favor osteomyelitis.

Why correct:

  • MRI is the investigation of choice (IOC) for differentiating Charcot joint from osteomyelitis.

  • It can accurately assess both bone and soft tissue involvement.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • ক) PET scan: Can help in difficult cases but is not the first-line investigation.

  • খ) CT scan: Better for bony architecture, but inferior to MRI for evaluating bone marrow and soft tissue infection.

  • গ) X-ray: Useful as an initial investigation but cannot reliably distinguish Charcot arthropathy from osteomyelitis, especially in early disease.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • IOC for differentiating Charcot joint from osteomyelitis: MRI.

  • Initial investigation: Plain X-ray.

  • MRI findings favoring osteomyelitis: Bone marrow edema contiguous with an ulcer, cortical destruction, abscess, sinus tract.

  • Charcot joint features: Joint subluxation/dislocation, fragmentation, deformity, multiple periarticular bone involvement with relatively intact overlying soft tissues.

  • Common MCQ trap: X-ray is the initial test, but MRI is the best investigation for differentiation.

Exam Pearl

In a diabetic foot, MRI is the investigation of choice to differentiate Charcot neuroarthropathy from osteomyelitis.

Medicine-06.question: ১৫) Pathognomic for diabetic kidney diseas in renal biopsy
Medicine-06.exp:
The pathognomonic histopathological finding of diabetic kidney disease (diabetic nephropathy) is the Kimmelstiel–Wilson nodule, also known as nodular glomerulosclerosis. It results from mesangial matrix expansion due to chronic hyperglycemia, leading to characteristic PAS-positive nodules within the glomeruli.

Why correct:

  • Kimmelstiel–Wilson nodules are pathognomonic for diabetic nephropathy.

  • They are typically seen in long-standing diabetes mellitus with persistent proteinuria.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • ক) Apple green birefringence: Characteristic of amyloidosis on Congo red staining under polarized light.

  • খ) Crescent moon shaped glomeruli: Seen in rapidly progressive (crescentic) glomerulonephritis (RPGN).

  • ঘ) Wire looping of capillaries: Characteristic of lupus nephritis (Class IV) due to subendothelial immune complex deposition.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Pathognomonic lesion: Kimmelstiel–Wilson nodules (nodular glomerulosclerosis).

  • Other renal biopsy findings: Thickened glomerular basement membrane (GBM), diffuse mesangial expansion, hyaline arteriolosclerosis (both afferent and efferent arterioles).

  • Earliest clinical marker: Microalbuminuria (30–300 mg/day).

  • Screening test: Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR).

  • Common MCQ trap: Kimmelstiel–Wilson nodules = Diabetic nephropathy; Apple-green birefringence = Amyloidosis.

Exam Pearl

"Kimmelstiel–Wilson nodules are pathognomonic of diabetic nephropathy, while microalbuminuria is its earliest clinical manifestation."

Medicine-06.question: ১৬) Which anti diabetic drugs act on proximal tubules ?
Medicine-06.exp:
Empagliflozin is an SGLT-2 (Sodium-Glucose Cotransporter-2) inhibitor that acts on the proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) of the kidney. It blocks glucose and sodium reabsorption, leading to glycosuria, reduced blood glucose levels, mild osmotic diuresis, and weight loss. It also provides significant cardiovascular and renal protection in patients with Type 2 diabetes.

Why correct:

  • Empagliflozin specifically inhibits SGLT-2 in the proximal renal tubules.

  • It lowers blood glucose independently of insulin.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • ক) Voglibose: An α-glucosidase inhibitor that acts in the intestinal brush border, delaying carbohydrate absorption.

  • গ) Saxagliptin: A DPP-4 inhibitor that increases endogenous GLP-1 and GIP levels; it does not act on the renal tubules.

  • ঘ) Meglitinides: Stimulate insulin secretion from pancreatic β-cells by closing ATP-sensitive potassium channels.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Drug acting on proximal tubule: SGLT-2 inhibitors (Empagliflozin, Dapagliflozin, Canagliflozin).

  • Site of action: Proximal convoluted tubule (S1 segment).

  • Mechanism: Blocks SGLT-2 → ↓ glucose reabsorption → ↑ urinary glucose excretion.

  • Benefits: Weight loss, mild BP reduction, cardiovascular and renal protection.

  • Adverse effects: Genital mycotic infections, UTIs, volume depletion, euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis (rare).

  • Common MCQ trap: SGLT-2 inhibitors act on the kidney, whereas DPP-4 inhibitors and meglitinides do not.

Exam Pearl

**Remember: "Gliflozins act in the Glomerular kidney tubules." SGLT-2 inhibitors (e.g., Empagliflozin) act on the proximal convoluted tubule to produce glycosuria.

Medicine-06.question: ১৭) Antidiabetic drug related to increased body weight
Medicine-06.exp:
Sulphonylureas cause weight gain by stimulating pancreatic β-cells to secrete insulin. The increased insulin promotes glucose uptake, lipogenesis, and fat storage, leading to increased body weight. They are also associated with a higher risk of hypoglycemia.

Why correct:

  • Sulphonylureas (e.g., Gliclazide, Glimepiride, Glibenclamide) are well known to cause weight gain.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • খ) Metformin: Usually causes weight loss or is weight-neutral; it is the preferred first-line drug in overweight patients.

  • গ) DPP-4 inhibitors: Generally weight-neutral (e.g., Sitagliptin, Saxagliptin).

  • ঘ) GLP-1 receptor agonists: Cause weight loss by reducing appetite and delaying gastric emptying (e.g., Liraglutide, Semaglutide).

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Drugs causing weight gain: Sulphonylureas, Insulin, Thiazolidinediones (Pioglitazone).

  • Weight-neutral drugs: Metformin (may cause slight weight loss), DPP-4 inhibitors.

  • Drugs causing weight loss: GLP-1 receptor agonists and SGLT-2 inhibitors.

  • Sulphonylurea mechanism: Closes ATP-sensitive K⁺ channels in pancreatic β-cells → ↑ insulin secretion.

  • Common adverse effects of sulphonylureas: Hypoglycemia and weight gain.

  • Common MCQ trap: GLP-1 receptor agonists reduce weight, whereas Sulphonylureas increase weight.

Exam Pearl

Remember the weight effects of antidiabetic drugs: Sulphonylureas, Insulin, and Pioglitazone → Weight gain; Metformin, GLP-1 receptor agonists, and SGLT-2 inhibitors → Weight loss/weight neutral.

Medicine-06.question: ১৮) Most common cause of thyrotoxicosis
Medicine-06.exp:
Graves' disease is the most common cause of thyrotoxicosis worldwide, especially in iodine-sufficient areas. It is an autoimmune disorder in which TSH receptor-stimulating antibodies (TSI/TRAb) stimulate the thyroid gland, causing excessive production of T₃ and T₄.

Why correct:

  • Graves' disease accounts for 60–80% of cases of thyrotoxicosis.

  • It is characterized by diffuse toxic goiter, ophthalmopathy, and sometimes pretibial myxedema.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • খ) Hashimoto's thyroiditis: Usually causes hypothyroidism. A transient thyrotoxic phase (Hashitoxicosis) may occur but is not the commonest cause.

  • গ) Multinodular goiter: Causes toxic multinodular goiter, a common cause in the elderly and iodine-deficient areas, but less common overall than Graves' disease.

  • ঘ) Subacute thyroiditis: Causes transient thyrotoxicosis due to release of preformed thyroid hormones; it is an uncommon cause.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Most common cause of thyrotoxicosis: Graves' disease.

  • Etiology: Autoimmune (TSH receptor-stimulating antibodies).

  • Classical triad: Diffuse goiter + Ophthalmopathy + Thyrotoxicosis.

  • Laboratory findings: ↓ TSH, ↑ Free T₄/T₃, positive TRAb/TSI.

  • Radioactive iodine uptake: Diffuse increased uptake in Graves' disease.

  • Common MCQ trap: Most common cause of thyrotoxicosis = Graves' disease; Most common cause in elderly = Toxic multinodular goiter.

Exam Pearl

Graves' disease is the most common cause of thyrotoxicosis, whereas toxic multinodular goiter is a more common cause in elderly patients.

Medicine-06.question: ১৯) Serum enzyme raised in hypothyroidism
Medicine-06.exp:
In hypothyroidism, AST (Aspartate aminotransferase) may be mildly elevated due to skeletal muscle involvement (hypothyroid myopathy) rather than liver disease. Muscle injury also causes elevation of creatine kinase (CK), which is the most commonly elevated enzyme in hypothyroidism.

Why correct:

  • AST is present in both liver and skeletal muscle.

  • Hypothyroid myopathy leads to muscle enzyme release, causing a rise in AST.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • ক) ALT: More specific for liver injury; not typically elevated in hypothyroidism.

  • গ) ALP: Usually normal or decreased in hypothyroidism because of reduced bone turnover.

  • ঘ) GGT: Marker of hepatobiliary disease or alcohol use; not a feature of hypothyroidism.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Most commonly elevated enzyme in hypothyroidism: Creatine kinase (CK).

  • Other enzymes that may increase: AST, LDH.

  • Mechanism: Hypothyroid myopathy causing muscle injury.

  • ALP: Often normal or low in hypothyroidism.

  • Common MCQ trap: If CK is not an option, choose AST.

Exam Pearl

Hypothyroidism commonly causes elevated CK; if CK is absent from the options, AST is the best answer due to hypothyroid myopathy.

Medicine-06.question: ২০) Measurement of serum level is unhelpful in hypothyroidism
Medicine-06.exp:
Serum T3 measurement is least helpful in diagnosing hypothyroidism because T3 levels are often maintained within the normal range until late in the disease due to increased peripheral conversion of T4 to T3. Therefore, TSH and Free T4 are the primary tests used for diagnosis.

Why correct:

  • T3 is often normal in early hypothyroidism, making it an unreliable diagnostic marker.

  • Primary hypothyroidism: ↑ TSH + ↓ Free T4 is the characteristic pattern.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • ক) TSH: Most sensitive and best initial test for primary hypothyroidism.

  • গ) T4: Free T4 confirms hypothyroidism and helps assess severity.

  • ঘ) All of them: Incorrect because TSH and T4 are essential in diagnosis.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Best screening test: Serum TSH.

  • Best confirmatory test: Free T4.

  • Least useful test: Total/Serum T3.

  • Primary hypothyroidism: ↑ TSH, ↓ Free T4.

  • Secondary hypothyroidism: ↓/Normal TSH, ↓ Free T4.

  • Common MCQ trap: T3 is usually normal in early hypothyroidism; therefore, it is not useful for diagnosis.

Exam Pearl

In hypothyroidism, always rely on TSH and Free T4; T3 is often normal and is the least useful investigation.

Medicine-06.question: ২১) In subacute thyroiditis radio iodine uptake is
Medicine-06.exp:
Subacute thyroiditis (De Quervain thyroiditis) is a destructive inflammatory disorder of the thyroid, usually following a viral infection. The initial thyrotoxic phase occurs due to release of preformed thyroid hormones from damaged thyroid follicles rather than increased hormone synthesis. Therefore, the thyroid does not actively take up iodine, resulting in low radioactive iodine uptake (RAIU).

Why correct:

  • Low RAI uptake is the characteristic finding in subacute thyroiditis because hormone synthesis is suppressed.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • ক) High: Seen in Graves' disease and toxic multinodular goiter, where thyroid hormone synthesis is increased.

  • গ) Variable: RAI uptake is characteristically low, not variable.

  • ঘ) Normal: Not seen during the thyrotoxic phase of subacute thyroiditis.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Subacute (De Quervain) thyroiditis: Painful, tender thyroid, often follows a viral illness.

  • Thyroid function: Initial thyrotoxicosis → transient hypothyroidism → recovery.

  • Radioactive iodine uptake (RAIU): Low.

  • ESR: Markedly elevated.

  • Treatment: NSAIDs; glucocorticoids if symptoms are severe.

  • Common MCQ trap: Graves' disease → High RAI uptake; Subacute thyroiditis → Low RAI uptake.

Exam Pearl

Low radioactive iodine uptake in a patient with thyrotoxicosis strongly suggests subacute thyroiditis rather than Graves' disease.

Medicine-06.question: ২২) Most commonly used antithyroid drug
Medicine-06.exp:
Carbimazole is the most commonly used antithyroid drug for the treatment of hyperthyroidism, especially Graves' disease. It is a prodrug that is converted to Methimazole, which inhibits thyroid peroxidase, thereby blocking the iodination and coupling of tyrosine residues and reducing the synthesis of T₃ and T₄.

Why correct:

  • Carbimazole is the first-line antithyroid drug in most patients because of its once-daily dosing, better safety profile, and longer duration of action.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • ক) Carbamazepine: An antiepileptic drug; has no role in treating hyperthyroidism.

  • গ) Propylthiouracil (PTU): Also an antithyroid drug but is not routinely first-line due to the risk of severe hepatotoxicity. It is preferred in the first trimester of pregnancy and thyroid storm.

  • ঘ) Levothyroxine: Used for hypothyroidism, not hyperthyroidism.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Most commonly used antithyroid drug: Carbimazole (Methimazole).

  • Mechanism: Inhibits thyroid peroxidase → ↓ synthesis of T₃ and T₄.

  • PTU advantage: Also inhibits peripheral conversion of T₄ to T₃.

  • PTU indications: First trimester of pregnancy and thyroid storm.

  • Major adverse effects: Agranulocytosis, rash; PTU may cause hepatotoxicity.

  • Common MCQ trap: Carbimazole = routine first-line; PTU = pregnancy (1st trimester) & thyroid storm.

Exam Pearl

For hyperthyroidism, Carbimazole is the routine first-line antithyroid drug, while PTU is reserved mainly for first-trimester pregnancy and thyroid storm.

Medicine-06.question: ২৩) The most common enzyme defect found in congenital adrenal hyperplasia
Medicine-06.exp:
21-hydroxylase deficiency is the most common enzyme defect causing Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (CAH), accounting for 90–95% of cases. It is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the CYP21A2 gene. Deficiency of 21-hydroxylase results in decreased cortisol (and often aldosterone) synthesis, leading to increased ACTH secretion and adrenal hyperplasia. The accumulated precursors are diverted to androgen synthesis, causing virilization.

Why correct:

  • 21-hydroxylase deficiency is the commonest cause of CAH.

  • 17-hydroxyprogesterone (17-OHP) is markedly elevated and is the screening test for this disorder.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • ক) 17-OH-Pregnenolone: This is a steroid intermediate, not an enzyme.

  • গ) 17-hydroxylase: Its deficiency causes a rare form of CAH characterized by hypertension, hypokalemia, and sexual infantilism, not the common form.

  • ঘ) 17-OH-Progesterone: This is also a steroid intermediate, not an enzyme; its level is elevated in 21-hydroxylase deficiency.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Most common CAH enzyme defect: 21-hydroxylase deficiency (90–95%).

  • Inheritance: Autosomal recessive.

  • Hormonal changes: ↓ Cortisol, ↓ Aldosterone (classic form), ↑ ACTH, ↑ Androgens.

  • Diagnostic marker: ↑ 17-hydroxyprogesterone.

  • Clinical features: Salt-wasting crisis, hypotension, hyperkalemia, virilization in females, precocious puberty in males.

  • Common MCQ trap: 21-hydroxylase is the enzyme, whereas 17-hydroxyprogesterone is the diagnostic marker, not the enzyme defect.

Exam Pearl

Remember: 21-hydroxylase deficiency is the commonest cause of CAH, and elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone is its hallmark laboratory finding.

Medicine-06.question: ২৪) Best investigation for confirming Cushing’s disease
Medicine-06.option4: Bilateral inferior petrosal sinus sampling with measurement of ACTH
Medicine-06.exp:
Cushing's disease refers to ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma causing hypercortisolism. After confirming Cushing's syndrome, the gold standard for confirming that the source of excess ACTH is the pituitary is Bilateral Inferior Petrosal Sinus Sampling (BIPSS) with simultaneous ACTH measurement.

Why correct:

  • BIPSS is the gold standard for confirming Cushing's disease and differentiating it from ectopic ACTH syndrome, especially when MRI findings are inconclusive.

  • It demonstrates a central-to-peripheral ACTH gradient, confirming a pituitary source.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • ক) High-dose dexamethasone suppression test: Supports the diagnosis of pituitary Cushing's disease but is less accurate than BIPSS.

  • খ) 24-hour urinary free cortisol level: Used to confirm Cushing's syndrome, but cannot identify the cause.

  • গ) Low-dose dexamethasone suppression test: A screening/diagnostic test for Cushing's syndrome, not for confirming Cushing's disease.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Cushing's syndrome: Clinical state due to excess cortisol.

  • Cushing's disease: Pituitary ACTH-secreting adenoma.

  • Screening/initial tests: 24-hour urinary free cortisol, low-dose dexamethasone suppression test, late-night salivary cortisol.

  • Test to differentiate pituitary from ectopic ACTH: High-dose dexamethasone suppression test (older test).

  • Gold standard for confirming Cushing's disease: Bilateral Inferior Petrosal Sinus Sampling (BIPSS).

  • Common MCQ trap: 24-hour urinary cortisol confirms Cushing's syndrome, whereas BIPSS confirms pituitary (Cushing's disease).

Exam Pearl

Remember: Low-dose DST and 24-hour urinary free cortisol diagnose Cushing's syndrome, but BIPSS is the gold standard for confirming Cushing's disease (pituitary source).

Medicine-06.question: ২৫) Most useful drug in case of phaeochromocytoma is
Medicine-06.exp:
Phenoxybenzamine is the drug of choice for preoperative medical management of pheochromocytoma. It is a non-selective, irreversible α-adrenergic blocker that controls hypertension and prevents catecholamine-induced hypertensive crises before surgical removal of the tumor.

Why correct:

  • Phenoxybenzamine provides long-lasting α-blockade, making it the preferred preoperative drug.

  • α-blockade must always be established before β-blockade to avoid unopposed α-adrenergic vasoconstriction and severe hypertension.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • ক) Phentolamine: A short-acting, reversible α-blocker mainly used in hypertensive emergencies due to pheochromocytoma, not for routine preoperative preparation.

  • খ) Doxazosin: A selective α₁-blocker; can be used as an alternative but is not the classical drug of choice in exams.

  • গ) Propranolol: A β-blocker. It should never be started before α-blockade, as it may precipitate a hypertensive crisis due to unopposed α-adrenergic stimulation.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Tumor: Catecholamine-secreting tumor of chromaffin cells.

  • Classic triad: Headache, sweating, palpitations.

  • Best initial biochemical test: Plasma free metanephrines (or 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines).

  • Definitive treatment: Surgical adrenalectomy.

  • Preoperative drug of choice: Phenoxybenzamine.

  • β-blocker: Added only after adequate α-blockade if tachycardia persists.

  • Common MCQ trap: Never give a β-blocker before an α-blocker in pheochromocytoma.

Exam Pearl

**For pheochromocytoma: Phenoxybenzamine first, β-blocker later. Remember: "α before β" to prevent hypertensive crisis.

Medicine-06.question: ২৬) Both Renin & aldosterone level is low in
Medicine-06.exp:
Liddle's syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by a gain-of-function mutation of the epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) in the distal nephron. This results in excessive sodium reabsorption, leading to hypertension, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis. The increased sodium retention suppresses the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS), causing both renin and aldosterone levels to be low.

Why correct:

  • Liddle's syndrome: ↓ Renin + ↓ Aldosterone due to autonomous ENaC activation.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • খ) Renal artery stenosis: Reduced renal perfusion causes ↑ Renin → ↑ Aldosterone (secondary hyperaldosteronism).

  • গ) Bartter's syndrome: Salt wasting leads to ↑ Renin + ↑ Aldosterone.

  • ঘ) Conn's syndrome (Primary hyperaldosteronism): ↓ Renin but ↑ Aldosterone.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Liddle's syndrome: ↓ Renin, ↓ Aldosterone, hypertension, hypokalemia.

  • Defect: Gain-of-function mutation of ENaC.

  • Treatment: Amiloride or Triamterene (ENaC blockers); spironolactone is ineffective.

  • Conn's syndrome: ↓ Renin, ↑ Aldosterone.

  • Renal artery stenosis & Bartter's syndrome: ↑ Renin, ↑ Aldosterone.

  • Common MCQ trap: Liddle's syndrome mimics hyperaldosteronism but aldosterone is low.

Exam Pearl

Liddle's syndrome = "Pseudo-hyperaldosteronism": Hypertension + Hypokalemia with low renin and low aldosterone; treat with Amiloride, not spironolactone.

Medicine-06.question: ২৭) A 27 year old female who is 14 weeks into her first pregnancy is investigated for excessive sweating and tremor. Blood test reveals the following : TSH < 0.05mu/ l, T4 188 nmol/l. What is the most appropriate management. ?
Medicine-06.option3: Surgery at start of third trimester
Medicine-06.exp:
This 27-year-old pregnant woman (14 weeks gestation) has thyrotoxicosis (TSH suppressed, T4 elevated) requiring treatment.

Although Methimazole/Carbimazole is generally the preferred antithyroid drug, PTU is the drug of choice during the first trimester of pregnancy because Methimazole/Carbimazole is associated with congenital malformations (methimazole embryopathy).

Since this patient is 14 weeks pregnant (around the beginning of the second trimester), current guidelines recommend switching from PTU to Methimazole/Carbimazole after the first trimester to reduce the risk of PTU-induced hepatotoxicity.

Therefore, the most appropriate management at 14 weeks is to start/switch to Carbimazole (Methimazole). However, if the exam follows the traditional teaching of "pregnancy = PTU", PTU may be expected. The exact answer depends on the options provided.

Why correct (current guideline):

  • ≤12–13 weeks (1st trimester): PTU.

  • After 1st trimester (≥13–16 weeks): Switch to Carbimazole/Methimazole.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • First trimester: PTU (avoids methimazole embryopathy).

  • Second & third trimester: Methimazole/Carbimazole (lower risk of hepatotoxicity).

  • Treatment goal: Maintain Free T4 at the upper limit of normal using the lowest effective dose.

  • Radioactive iodine: Contraindicated in pregnancy.

  • Surgery: Consider in the second trimester if antithyroid drugs are ineffective or contraindicated.

  • Common MCQ trap: Read the gestational age carefully. 14 weeks = second trimester → Carbimazole/Methimazole according to current guidelines.

Exam Pearl

Pregnancy + Hyperthyroidism: PTU in the first trimester, then switch to Methimazole/Carbimazole in the second and third trimesters. If the question simply says "pregnant" without gestational age, many exams expect PTU.

Medicine-06.question: ২৮) Which types of thyroid cancer is associated with Hashimoto’s thyroiditis ?
Medicine-06.exp:
Hashimoto's thyroiditis is a chronic autoimmune lymphocytic thyroiditis and is classically associated with Primary Thyroid Lymphoma, especially B-cell Non-Hodgkin lymphoma (MALT lymphoma/Diffuse Large B-cell Lymphoma). Chronic lymphocytic infiltration of the thyroid predisposes to the development of lymphoma.

Why correct:

  • Lymphoma is the classical and strongest malignant association of Hashimoto's thyroiditis.

  • Patients typically present with a rapidly enlarging thyroid swelling on a background of long-standing Hashimoto's thyroiditis.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • ক) Follicular carcinoma: No significant association with Hashimoto's thyroiditis.

  • গ) Medullary carcinoma: Arises from parafollicular (C) cells and is associated with MEN 2 syndrome.

  • ঘ) Papillary carcinoma: May coexist with Hashimoto's thyroiditis, but the classical exam association is thyroid lymphoma.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Hashimoto's thyroiditis: Most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient areas.

  • Associated malignancy: Primary thyroid lymphoma (most important MCQ association).

  • Autoantibodies: Anti-TPO (most sensitive), Anti-thyroglobulin.

  • Histology: Hürthle cells, lymphoid follicles with germinal centers.

  • Common MCQ trap: Hashimoto's → Lymphoma; Radiation exposure → Papillary carcinoma; MEN 2 → Medullary carcinoma.

Exam Pearl

Remember the classic association: Hashimoto's thyroiditis → Primary thyroid lymphoma (B-cell Non-Hodgkin lymphoma).

Medicine-06.question: ২৯) A 60 year old female is admitted to hospital with a severe pneumonia. Patient have no clinical evidence of thyroid disease. Thyroid function tests are most likely to show
Medicine-06.option1: Raised T4 , Raised T3 , low serum TSH
Medicine-06.option2: Low T4, low T3 , raised serum TSH
Medicine-06.option3: Raised T4 , raised T3 , raised serum TSH
Medicine-06.option4: Raised T4 , Normal / low T3 , low serum TSH
Medicine-06.exp:
This patient has severe pneumonia with no clinical evidence of thyroid disease, suggesting Non-thyroidal illness syndrome (NTIS), also known as Euthyroid Sick Syndrome (ESS).

During severe systemic illness:

  • Peripheral conversion of T4 to T3 decreases due to reduced 5'-deiodinase activity.

  • Therefore, T3 falls first (most consistent finding).

  • TSH is usually low or normal during the acute phase.

  • T4 may be normal or transiently increased early, but may decrease in prolonged severe illness.

Among the given options, Raised T4 + Normal/Low T3 + Low TSH is the best answer.

Why correct:

  • Acute severe illness causes decreased T3 with suppressed/normal TSH.

  • This pattern is consistent with Euthyroid Sick Syndrome.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • ক) Raised T4, Raised T3, Low TSH: T3 is not elevated in euthyroid sick syndrome.

  • খ) Low T4, Low T3, Raised TSH: Raised TSH suggests primary hypothyroidism, not acute illness.

  • গ) Raised T4, Raised T3, Raised TSH: Not compatible with euthyroid sick syndrome or any common thyroid disorder.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Condition: Euthyroid Sick Syndrome (Non-thyroidal illness syndrome).

  • Common causes: Sepsis, pneumonia, trauma, surgery, myocardial infarction.

  • Earliest hormonal change: ↓ T3.

  • TSH: Usually normal or low during acute illness; may rise slightly during recovery.

  • Reverse T3 (rT3): Increased due to reduced conversion of T4 to T3.

  • Treatment: Treat the underlying illness; thyroid hormone replacement is not routinely indicated.

  • Common MCQ trap: Low T3 is the hallmark of euthyroid sick syndrome.

Exam Pearl

The hallmark of Euthyroid Sick Syndrome is low T3 with increased reverse T3; thyroid function usually normalizes after recovery from the underlying illness.

Medicine-06.question: ৩০) Antibodies to thyroid peroxidase is most prevalent in
Medicine-06.exp:
Anti-thyroid peroxidase (Anti-TPO) antibodies are most commonly and most strongly associated with autoimmune hypothyroidism (Hashimoto's thyroiditis). These antibodies target the thyroid peroxidase enzyme, leading to destruction of thyroid follicles and progressive hypothyroidism.

Why correct:

  • Hashimoto's thyroiditis has the highest prevalence of Anti-TPO antibodies (present in about 90–95% of patients).

  • It is the most sensitive serological marker for autoimmune hypothyroidism.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • ক) Multinodular goitre: Not an autoimmune disease; Anti-TPO antibodies are usually absent.

  • খ) Graves' disease: Anti-TPO antibodies may be present in 70–80% of cases, but the characteristic antibody is TSH receptor antibody (TRAb/TSI).

  • গ) Transient thyroiditis: Anti-TPO antibodies may be present in some autoimmune forms (e.g., postpartum thyroiditis), but their prevalence is lower than in Hashimoto's thyroiditis.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Most sensitive antibody for Hashimoto's thyroiditis: Anti-TPO antibody.

  • Most specific antibody for Graves' disease: TSH receptor antibody (TRAb/TSI).

  • Hashimoto's thyroiditis: ↑ Anti-TPO, ↑ Anti-thyroglobulin, hypothyroidism, Hürthle cells.

  • Graves' disease: ↑ TRAb (TSI), diffuse toxic goiter, ophthalmopathy.

  • Common MCQ trap: Anti-TPO is present in both Hashimoto's and Graves', but it is most prevalent in Hashimoto's thyroiditis.

Exam Pearl

Remember: Hashimoto's thyroiditis → Anti-TPO antibody (most prevalent); Graves' disease → TSH receptor antibody (TRAb/TSI).

Medicine-06.question: ৩১) Features of PCOS
Medicine-06.exp:
Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS) is characterized by chronic anovulation, hyperandrogenism, and polycystic ovaries. The typical hormonal profile shows increased LH, normal or low FSH, and insulin resistance with hyperinsulinemia.

Assessment of the options:

  • ক) High serum prolactin: May be mildly elevated in a few patients but is not a typical feature of PCOS.

  • খ) Primary amenorrhoea: PCOS usually causes secondary amenorrhoea or oligomenorrhoea, not primary amenorrhoea.

  • গ) Low serum LH: Incorrect. LH is usually elevated, with an increased LH:FSH ratio (classically >2:1, though not essential for diagnosis).

  • ঘ) Hypoglycaemia: Incorrect. PCOS is associated with insulin resistance and hyperinsulinemia, not hypoglycaemia.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Cardinal features: Hyperandrogenism, oligo-/anovulation, polycystic ovaries.

  • Menstrual abnormality: Oligomenorrhoea or secondary amenorrhoea.

  • Hormonal changes: ↑ LH, normal/↓ FSH, ↑ androgens.

  • Metabolic association: Insulin resistance, obesity, increased risk of type 2 diabetes.

  • Diagnosis: Rotterdam criteria (any 2 of 3: oligo/anovulation, hyperandrogenism, polycystic ovaries on ultrasound).

  • Common MCQ trap: PCOS causes hyperinsulinemia, not hypoglycaemia, and secondary, not primary, amenorrhoea.

Exam Pearl

Think of PCOS as: Hyperandrogenism + Oligomenorrhoea/Secondary amenorrhoea + Insulin resistance + Increased LH (not low LH).

Medicine-06.question: ৩২) Risk factors for relapse of Graves’ disease
Medicine-06.exp:
Relapse of Graves' disease is common after stopping antithyroid drugs, especially if remission has not been achieved. The risk of relapse is higher in patients with large goiter, high TRAb levels, severe hyperthyroidism, smoking, younger age, and short duration of therapy.

Why correct:

  • Cessation of antithyroid therapy is associated with a significant risk of recurrence of hyperthyroidism, particularly within the first year after treatment withdrawal.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • ক) Absence of a goitre: Incorrect. A large goiter increases the risk of relapse.

  • গ) Female sex: Graves' disease is more common in females, but male sex is associated with a higher relapse risk.

  • ঘ) Older age: Younger age is associated with a greater risk of relapse.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Risk factors for relapse: Large goiter, high TRAb titre, severe hyperthyroidism, smoking, younger age, male sex, short duration of antithyroid therapy.

  • Duration of antithyroid drug therapy: Usually 12–18 months.

  • Best predictor of relapse: Persistently elevated TRAb after treatment.

  • Common MCQ trap: Large goiter, not absence of goiter, predicts relapse.

Exam Pearl

The strongest predictor of Graves' disease relapse is a persistently elevated TSH receptor antibody (TRAb) level after completion of antithyroid therapy.

Medicine-06.question: ৩৩) Antidiabetic drug with risk of hypoglycemia
Medicine-06.exp:
Sulphonylureas are the antidiabetic drugs with the highest risk of hypoglycemia because they stimulate insulin secretion from pancreatic β-cells irrespective of blood glucose level. The risk is greater in elderly patients, those with renal impairment, and with long-acting sulphonylureas (e.g., glibenclamide).

Why correct:

  • Sulphonylureas (e.g., Gliclazide, Glimepiride, Glibenclamide) increase insulin release continuously, predisposing to hypoglycemia.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • খ) Metformin: Does not stimulate insulin secretion; therefore, hypoglycemia is rare when used alone.

  • গ) DPP-4 inhibitors: Have a very low risk of hypoglycemia because they enhance glucose-dependent insulin secretion.

  • ঘ) GLP-1 receptor agonists: Also stimulate glucose-dependent insulin release and have a low risk of hypoglycemia when used alone.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Highest risk of hypoglycemia: Sulphonylureas and Insulin.

  • Sulphonylurea mechanism: Closes ATP-sensitive K⁺ channels on pancreatic β-cells → ↑ insulin secretion.

  • Examples: Gliclazide, Glimepiride, Glibenclamide.

  • Drugs with minimal hypoglycemia risk: Metformin, DPP-4 inhibitors, GLP-1 receptor agonists, SGLT-2 inhibitors.

  • Common MCQ trap: Metformin is first-line and rarely causes hypoglycemia when used as monotherapy.

Exam Pearl

Whenever asked which oral antidiabetic drug causes hypoglycemia, think Sulphonylureas (especially Glibenclamide).

Medicine-06.question: ৩৪) Most common adverse effect of antithyroid drugs
Medicine-06.exp:
Skin rash is the most common adverse effect of antithyroid drugs (Carbimazole, Methimazole, and Propylthiouracil). It is usually mild, presenting as a pruritic maculopapular rash or urticaria, and often resolves with antihistamines or by changing the drug if necessary.

Why correct:

  • Rash is the commonest adverse effect of thionamides.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • খ) Agranulocytosis: A rare but life-threatening adverse effect (≈0.2–0.5%). Patients should stop the drug immediately if they develop fever or sore throat.

  • গ) Hypothyroidism: May occur due to over-treatment, but it is not the most common adverse effect.

  • ঘ) Hypocalcaemia: Associated with thyroid surgery, not with antithyroid drugs.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Most common adverse effect: Skin rash (maculopapular/urticarial).

  • Most serious adverse effect: Agranulocytosis.

  • Major PTU-specific adverse effect: Severe hepatotoxicity.

  • Major Methimazole/Carbimazole-specific concern: Teratogenicity (first trimester of pregnancy).

  • Patient advice: If fever or sore throat develops while taking antithyroid drugs, stop the drug immediately and check a complete blood count (CBC).

  • Common MCQ trap: Most common = Rash; Most dangerous = Agranulocytosis.

Exam Pearl

Remember: Antithyroid drugs → Most common adverse effect = Rash; Most feared adverse effect = Agranulocytosis.

Medicine-06.question: ৩৫) Most common causes of death in diabetes
Medicine-06.exp:
Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the most common cause of death in patients with diabetes mellitus. Chronic hyperglycemia accelerates atherosclerosis, increasing the risk of coronary artery disease (CAD), myocardial infarction (MI), stroke, and peripheral arterial disease.

Why correct:

  • Coronary artery disease is the leading cause of mortality in both Type 1 and Type 2 diabetes, especially Type 2 DM.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • ক) Renal failure: A major microvascular complication and cause of morbidity, but not the leading cause of death.

  • খ) Hypoglycaemic attack: Can be fatal but is an uncommon cause of death.

  • গ) Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA): An acute complication, more common in Type 1 DM, but with modern treatment it is not the leading cause of mortality.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Most common cause of death in diabetes: Cardiovascular disease (especially CAD/MI).

  • Most common microvascular complications: Retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy.

  • Most common macrovascular complications: Coronary artery disease, stroke, peripheral arterial disease.

  • Risk factors for CVD in diabetes: Hypertension, dyslipidemia, smoking, obesity, poor glycemic control.

  • Common MCQ trap: Renal failure is the leading cause of end-stage renal disease (ESRD), but cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death in diabetics.

Exam Pearl

In diabetes mellitus, patients are more likely to die from cardiovascular disease (especially myocardial infarction) than from hyperglycemic emergencies or renal failure.

Medicine-06.question: ৩৬) Most common cause of Cushing’s syndrome
Medicine-06.exp:
The most common cause of Cushing's syndrome overall is iatrogenic, due to prolonged administration of exogenous glucocorticoids (e.g., prednisolone, dexamethasone). Long-term steroid therapy suppresses the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, resulting in features of hypercortisolism.

Why correct:

  • Iatrogenic (exogenous steroid use) is the commonest cause of Cushing's syndrome.

  • Cushing's disease specifically refers to ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma, which is the most common endogenous cause, not the most common overall.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • ক) Adrenal adenoma: A cause of endogenous Cushing's syndrome, but less common than iatrogenic causes.

  • খ) Adrenal carcinoma: A rare cause of Cushing's syndrome.

  • গ) Idiopathic: Not the most common cause.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Most common cause of Cushing's syndrome (overall): Iatrogenic (exogenous corticosteroids).

  • Most common endogenous cause: Cushing's disease (pituitary ACTH adenoma).

  • Most common ACTH-independent cause: Adrenal adenoma.

  • Clinical features: Central obesity, moon face, buffalo hump, purple striae, hypertension, diabetes, proximal muscle weakness.

  • Common MCQ trap: Overall → Iatrogenic; Endogenous → Cushing's disease.

Exam Pearl

Remember the distinction: Most common overall cause of Cushing's syndrome = Iatrogenic steroid therapy; Most common endogenous cause = Cushing's disease (pituitary ACTH adenoma).

Medicine-06.question: ৩৭) Which nerve compression is more common in diabetes?
Medicine-06.exp:
Median nerve compression causing Carpal Tunnel Syndrome (CTS) is the most common entrapment neuropathy in patients with diabetes mellitus. Chronic hyperglycemia leads to glycation of connective tissue, nerve ischemia, and edema, making the median nerve more susceptible to compression beneath the flexor retinaculum.

Why correct:

  • Median nerve entrapment (Carpal Tunnel Syndrome) is the commonest compressive neuropathy in diabetes.

  • Symptoms include numbness, tingling, and pain in the thumb, index, middle, and radial half of the ring finger, often worse at night.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • খ) Radial nerve: Compression is uncommon in diabetes.

  • গ) Lateral popliteal (common peroneal) nerve: May be compressed at the fibular neck but is less common than median nerve entrapment.

  • ঘ) Ulnar nerve: Can be affected but is less frequent than median nerve compression.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Most common entrapment neuropathy in diabetes: Median nerve (Carpal Tunnel Syndrome).

  • Most common diabetic neuropathy: Distal symmetrical sensorimotor polyneuropathy.

  • CTS clinical features: Nocturnal paresthesia, thenar weakness, positive Phalen's and Tinel's signs.

  • Diagnosis: Nerve conduction study (NCS) is the investigation of choice.

  • Common MCQ trap: Differentiate entrapment neuropathy (Median nerve) from distal symmetrical polyneuropathy.

Exam Pearl

In diabetes, the most common nerve compression syndrome is Median nerve compression (Carpal Tunnel Syndrome).

Medicine-06.question: ৩৮) Features of Cushing’s syndrome excludes
Medicine-06.exp:
Cushing's syndrome results from chronic excess cortisol. Cortisol increases vascular sensitivity to catecholamines, leading to hypertension, not hypotension. Therefore, hypotension is not a feature of Cushing's syndrome.

Why correct:

  • Hypotension is not seen in Cushing's syndrome; patients typically have hypertension.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • ক) Moon face: A classic feature due to redistribution of body fat.

  • গ) Hyperglycemia: Cortisol increases gluconeogenesis and causes insulin resistance, leading to hyperglycemia.

  • ঘ) Osteoporosis: Cortisol inhibits bone formation and increases bone resorption, resulting in osteoporosis.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Common features: Moon face, central obesity, buffalo hump, purple striae, proximal muscle weakness, hypertension, hyperglycemia, osteoporosis.

  • Electrolyte abnormality: Hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis (especially in ACTH-dependent disease).

  • Most common cause: Iatrogenic corticosteroid therapy.

  • Most common endogenous cause: Cushing's disease (pituitary ACTH adenoma).

  • Common MCQ trap: Cushing's syndrome causes hypertension, whereas Addison's disease causes hypotension.

Exam Pearl

Differentiate adrenal disorders: Cushing's syndrome → Hypertension + Hyperglycemia; Addison's disease → Hypotension + Hypoglycemia.

Medicine-06.question: ৩৯) Key substrate for thyroid hormone synthesis
Medicine-06.exp:
Iodide is the essential substrate required for the synthesis of thyroid hormones (T₃ and T₄). It is actively transported into thyroid follicular cells by the sodium-iodide symporter (NIS), oxidized by thyroid peroxidase (TPO), and incorporated into tyrosine residues of thyroglobulin to form MIT and DIT, which subsequently couple to produce T₃ and T₄.

Why correct:

  • Iodide is the primary raw material (substrate) for thyroid hormone synthesis.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • খ) MIT (Monoiodotyrosine): An intermediate formed during hormone synthesis, not the initial substrate.

  • গ) DIT (Diiodotyrosine): Also an intermediate; two DIT molecules couple to form T₄.

  • ঘ) FT₄ (Free thyroxine): It is the final hormone, not a substrate.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Key substrate: Iodide.

  • Key enzyme: Thyroid peroxidase (TPO).

  • Transporter: Sodium-iodide symporter (NIS).

  • Hormone synthesis: MIT + DIT = T₃; DIT + DIT = T₄.

  • Common MCQ trap: Iodide is the substrate, whereas MIT and DIT are intermediates.

Exam Pearl

Remember the sequence: Iodide → MIT/DIT → T₃ & T₄. Iodide is the essential substrate for thyroid hormone synthesis.

Medicine-06.question: ৪০) Most useful investigation of thyroid function
Medicine-06.exp:
Serum TSH is the most useful single test for assessing thyroid function because it is the most sensitive marker of thyroid hormone status. Small changes in circulating T₄ produce large changes in TSH through the hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis.

Why correct:

  • TSH is the best screening test for both hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism in patients with an intact pituitary gland.

  • It detects thyroid dysfunction earlier than T₃ or T₄.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • খ) T3: Least useful for diagnosing hypothyroidism because it often remains normal until late disease.

  • গ) T4: Useful for confirming thyroid dysfunction but less sensitive than TSH as a screening test.

  • ঘ) FT3: Helpful in selected cases (e.g., T3 thyrotoxicosis) but not the best overall test for thyroid function.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Most useful screening test for thyroid function: TSH.

  • Best test to confirm hypothyroidism: Free T4.

  • Least useful test in hypothyroidism: T3.

  • Primary hypothyroidism: ↑ TSH, ↓ FT4.

  • Primary hyperthyroidism: ↓ TSH, ↑ FT4/FT3.

  • Common MCQ trap: TSH is the best screening test, whereas Free T4 assesses the severity of thyroid dysfunction.

Exam Pearl

For thyroid function assessment, remember: TSH is the single most useful investigation; always interpret it together with Free T4 when abnormal.

Medicine-06.question: ৪১) Long-acting insulin preparation
Medicine-06.exp:
Insulin degludec is an ultra-long-acting insulin analogue used for basal insulin replacement in diabetes mellitus. It has a prolonged duration of action of more than 42 hours with a stable glucose-lowering effect.

Why correct:

  • Degludec is classified as a long-acting/ultra-long-acting insulin preparation.

  • It provides a steady basal insulin level with a lower risk of hypoglycemia compared with some older basal insulins.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • ক) Lispro: Rapid-acting insulin analogue; used around meal times.

  • খ) Aspart: Rapid-acting insulin analogue; used for prandial glucose control.

  • গ) Lente: Intermediate-acting insulin (not long-acting).

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Rapid-acting insulin: Lispro, Aspart, Glulisine → meal-time insulin.

  • Short-acting insulin: Regular insulin.

  • Intermediate-acting insulin: NPH, Lente.

  • Long-acting insulin: Glargine, Detemir.

  • Ultra-long-acting insulin: Degludec.

  • Common MCQ trap: Lente = intermediate acting; Degludec = ultra-long acting.

Exam Pearl

Remember insulin duration: Lispro/Aspart = Rapid, NPH/Lente = Intermediate, Glargine/Detemir/Degludec = Long acting (Degludec longest).

Medicine-06.question: ৪২) Disease with thyroid hormone deficiency
Medicine-06.exp:
Hashimoto’s thyroiditis is the most common cause of primary hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient areas. It is an autoimmune destruction of thyroid follicles caused mainly by anti-thyroid peroxidase (Anti-TPO) and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies, leading to reduced production of T₃ and T₄.

Why correct:

  • Hashimoto’s thyroiditis → thyroid hormone deficiency → hypothyroidism.

  • It causes gradual destruction of thyroid tissue and reduced thyroid hormone synthesis.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • ক) Graves’ disease: Causes excess thyroid hormone production (hyperthyroidism) due to TSH receptor antibodies.

  • গ) Multinodular goiter: Usually causes euthyroidism or may cause hyperthyroidism if toxic; not a typical cause of hormone deficiency.

  • ঘ) Subacute thyroiditis: Causes a transient hyperthyroid phase followed by possible temporary hypothyroidism, but is not the classic disease of thyroid hormone deficiency.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Hashimoto’s thyroiditis: Autoimmune destruction of thyroid gland.

  • Hormonal pattern: ↓ T₃/↓ T₄, ↑ TSH (primary hypothyroidism).

  • Most common antibody: Anti-TPO antibody.

  • Clinical features of hypothyroidism: Weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation, bradycardia, dry skin.

  • Graves’ disease: Hyperthyroidism + TSH receptor antibody (TRAb).

  • Common MCQ trap: Hashimoto’s = hypothyroidism; Graves’ = hyperthyroidism.

Exam Pearl

The classic thyroid hormone deficiency disorder is Hashimoto’s thyroiditis causing primary hypothyroidism.

Medicine-06.question: ৪৩) Thyroid tumor arising from parafollicular C cell
Medicine-06.exp:
Medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) arises from the parafollicular C cells of the thyroid gland. These cells produce calcitonin, which helps regulate calcium metabolism.

Why correct:

  • Medullary carcinoma originates from C cells (parafollicular cells).

  • It secretes calcitonin, which is a useful tumor marker.

  • It is associated with MEN 2 syndrome and RET proto-oncogene mutation.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • ক) Papillary carcinoma: Arises from follicular epithelial cells; associated with radiation exposure and lymphatic spread.

  • খ) Follicular carcinoma: Also arises from follicular cells; spreads mainly through blood vessels.

  • ঘ) Anaplastic tumor: A highly aggressive carcinoma arising from follicular epithelial cells, usually in elderly patients.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Medullary thyroid carcinoma: Parafollicular C cells.

  • Hormone/marker: Calcitonin.

  • Genetics: RET mutation.

  • Association: MEN 2A and MEN 2B.

  • Spread: Mainly lymphatic and hematogenous.

  • Common MCQ trap:

    • C cells → Medullary carcinoma → Calcitonin

    • Follicular cells → Papillary/Follicular carcinoma → Thyroid hormones

Exam Pearl

Remember: "C cells cause Calcitonin and Cancer = Medullary carcinoma."

Medicine-06.question: ৪৪) Major glucocorticoid in human
Medicine-06.exp:
Cortisol is the major glucocorticoid in humans produced by the zona fasciculata of the adrenal cortex. It plays an important role in stress response, metabolism, immune regulation, and maintenance of blood pressure.

Why correct:

  • Cortisol is the principal naturally occurring glucocorticoid in humans.

  • It increases gluconeogenesis, promotes protein catabolism, and has anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive effects.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • খ) Aldosterone: A mineralocorticoid produced by the zona glomerulosa; regulates sodium and potassium balance.

  • গ) Estradiol: A sex steroid (estrogen), mainly produced by ovaries.

  • ঘ) Corticosterone: Has glucocorticoid activity but is not the major glucocorticoid in humans.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Major glucocorticoid: Cortisol.

  • Site of synthesis: Zona fasciculata of adrenal cortex.

  • Major mineralocorticoid: Aldosterone.

  • Adrenal cortex layers (GFR):

    • Zona Glomerulosa → Aldosterone

    • Zona Fasciculata → Cortisol

    • Zona Reticularis → Androgens

  • Regulation: Hypothalamus (CRH) → Pituitary (ACTH) → Adrenal cortex (Cortisol).

  • Common MCQ trap: Aldosterone = mineralocorticoid; Cortisol = glucocorticoid.

Exam Pearl

Remember: "Fasciculata makes Cortisol" — the major glucocorticoid of humans is Cortisol.

Medicine-06.question: ৪৫) Which antidiabetic drug decreases plasma insulin level?
Medicine-06.exp:
Metformin is an antidiabetic drug that decreases plasma insulin levels by improving insulin sensitivity and reducing hepatic gluconeogenesis. Unlike insulin secretagogues, it does not stimulate pancreatic β-cells; therefore, circulating insulin levels may decrease or remain unchanged.

Why correct:

  • Metformin reduces hepatic glucose production and increases peripheral glucose uptake.

  • It improves insulin sensitivity, resulting in lower plasma insulin concentration (especially in insulin-resistant patients).

Why other options are incorrect:

  • ক) Sulphonylureas: Increase insulin secretion from pancreatic β-cells → increase plasma insulin level.

  • গ) DPP-4 inhibitors: Increase glucose-dependent insulin secretion → may increase insulin levels.

  • ঘ) GLP-1 receptor agonists: Stimulate glucose-dependent insulin release → increase insulin secretion.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Metformin mechanism:

    • ↓ Hepatic gluconeogenesis (main action)

    • ↑ Peripheral insulin sensitivity

    • ↓ Intestinal glucose absorption (minor effect)

  • Effect on insulin: Decreases/does not increase plasma insulin.

  • Weight effect: Usually weight neutral or weight loss.

  • Major adverse effect: Gastrointestinal upset; rare lactic acidosis.

  • Contraindication: Severe renal impairment.

  • Common MCQ trap:

    • Metformin → improves insulin sensitivity

    • Sulphonylureas → increase insulin secretion

Exam Pearl

The only major oral antidiabetic drug among these that lowers plasma insulin levels is Metformin because it improves insulin sensitivity rather than stimulating insulin release.

Medicine-06.question: ৪৬) Anaphylactic shock is mediated by
Medicine-06.exp:
Anaphylactic shock is a Type I (immediate) hypersensitivity reaction mediated by IgE antibodies. Exposure to an allergen causes IgE cross-linking on mast cells and basophils, leading to release of inflammatory mediators such as histamine, leukotrienes, and prostaglandins, resulting in vasodilation, increased vascular permeability, bronchoconstriction, and shock.

Why correct:

  • IgE binds to Fcε receptors on mast cells and basophils.

  • Re-exposure to the allergen causes mast cell degranulation, producing anaphylaxis.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • ক) IgG: Involved in Type II and Type III hypersensitivity reactions; not responsible for classic anaphylaxis.

  • খ) IgA: Mainly provides mucosal immunity and protection in secretions.

  • গ) IgM: First antibody produced in primary immune response; involved in complement activation, not anaphylaxis.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Anaphylaxis: Type I hypersensitivity reaction.

  • Antibody involved: IgE.

  • Main cells: Mast cells and basophils.

  • Major mediator: Histamine.

  • Clinical features: Hypotension, bronchospasm, urticaria, angioedema.

  • Emergency treatment: Intramuscular adrenaline (epinephrine).

  • Common MCQ trap:

    • Type I → IgE

    • Type II → IgG/IgM

    • Type III → Immune complexes

    • Type IV → T cells

Exam Pearl

Remember: Immediate allergy and anaphylaxis = IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation.

Medicine-06.question: ৪৭) Which drug does not induce diabetes mellitus?
Medicine-06.exp:
Several drugs can induce diabetes mellitus by causing insulin resistance, impairing insulin secretion, or damaging pancreatic β-cells. Among the given options, Sodium valproate is not a typical drug that induces diabetes mellitus.

Why correct:

  • Sodium valproate is an antiepileptic drug and is not classically associated with drug-induced diabetes mellitus.

  • It may cause other metabolic effects (e.g., weight gain), but it is not a recognized common cause of diabetes.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • খ) Phenytoin: Can cause hyperglycemia by impairing insulin secretion and is associated with glucose intolerance.

  • গ) Glucocorticoids: A major cause of steroid-induced diabetes due to increased insulin resistance and increased hepatic gluconeogenesis.

  • ঘ) Thiazide diuretic: Can cause impaired glucose tolerance by reducing insulin secretion and causing hypokalemia, which affects β-cell function.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Common drugs causing diabetes mellitus:

    • Glucocorticoids → ↑ insulin resistance (most important).

    • Thiazide diuretics → ↓ insulin secretion (via hypokalemia).

    • Phenytoin → impaired insulin release.

    • Atypical antipsychotics (e.g., clozapine, olanzapine) → metabolic syndrome.

  • Common MCQ trap: Not all drugs causing weight gain cause diabetes; focus on drugs affecting insulin action or secretion.

Exam Pearl

The classic drug causing diabetes mellitus is glucocorticoids; among the options, Sodium valproate is the exception.

Medicine-06.question: ৪৮) Commonest cause of cardiogenic shock
Medicine-06.exp:
Acute myocardial infarction (AMI) is the commonest cause of cardiogenic shock. Cardiogenic shock occurs when the heart is unable to maintain adequate tissue perfusion due to severe reduction in cardiac output. In AMI, extensive damage to the left ventricular myocardium causes severe impairment of contractility, leading to pump failure and shock.

Why correct:

  • AMI, especially a large anterior wall myocardial infarction, is the most common cause of cardiogenic shock.

  • It causes acute left ventricular failure with reduced cardiac output.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • খ) DCM (Dilated cardiomyopathy): Can cause chronic heart failure and cardiogenic shock, but is a less common cause compared with AMI.

  • গ) SVT (Supraventricular tachycardia): May cause hemodynamic instability if sustained, but rarely causes cardiogenic shock.

  • ঘ) AF (Atrial fibrillation): Can worsen cardiac function, especially in heart failure, but is not the commonest cause.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Cardiogenic shock: Failure of the heart as a pump → ↓ cardiac output with adequate/increased filling pressure.

  • Commonest cause: Acute myocardial infarction (AMI).

  • Most commonly affected ventricle: Left ventricle.

  • Clinical features: Hypotension, cold clammy skin, oliguria, altered mental state.

  • Hemodynamic findings: ↓ Cardiac output, ↑ systemic vascular resistance, ↑ pulmonary capillary wedge pressure.

  • Management principles: Revascularization (PCI), inotropes/vasopressors when required.

  • Common MCQ trap: AMI → Cardiogenic shock; Massive pulmonary embolism → Obstructive shock.

Exam Pearl

The most common cause of cardiogenic shock is Acute Myocardial Infarction (AMI) due to severe left ventricular pump failure.

Medicine-06.question: ৪৯) Which anti diabetic drugs have cardiovascular benefit?
Medicine-06.exp:
SGLT2 inhibitors have proven cardiovascular benefits in patients with type 2 diabetes, particularly by reducing the risk of heart failure hospitalization and providing cardiorenal protection. They work by inhibiting sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) in the proximal renal tubule, causing increased urinary glucose excretion.

Why correct:

  • SGLT2 inhibitors (e.g., Empagliflozin, Dapagliflozin, Canagliflozin) reduce cardiovascular events and heart failure risk.

  • They have additional benefits in chronic kidney disease (CKD).

Why other options are incorrect:

  • ক) Meglitinides: Increase insulin secretion but have no proven cardiovascular benefit.

  • খ) Alpha glucosidase inhibitors: Mainly reduce postprandial glucose rise; no significant cardiovascular protective effect.

  • ঘ) DPP-4 inhibitors: Generally cardiovascular neutral. Some (e.g., saxagliptin) may increase risk of heart failure hospitalization.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • Antidiabetic drugs with cardiovascular benefit:

    • SGLT2 inhibitors → ↓ heart failure hospitalization, cardiorenal protection.

    • GLP-1 receptor agonists → ↓ major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE).

  • Cardiovascular neutral: Metformin (generally considered neutral/possible benefit), DPP-4 inhibitors.

  • Main action of SGLT2 inhibitors: Block glucose reabsorption in proximal renal tubule → glycosuria.

  • Common MCQ trap: SGLT2 inhibitors = Heart failure benefit; GLP-1 agonists = Atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease benefit.

Exam Pearl

For diabetic patients with cardiovascular disease or heart failure risk, remember: SGLT2 inhibitors provide cardiovascular and renal protection.

Medicine-06.question: ৫০) Indicator of severe ketoacidosis
Medicine-06.exp:
Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) severity is assessed by clinical features and biochemical parameters. Blood ketone level > 6 mmol/L is an indicator of severe ketoacidosis.

Why correct:

  • Severe DKA is associated with marked ketonemia.

  • Blood ketones > 6 mmol/L indicates severe ketone accumulation and significant metabolic derangement.

Why other options are incorrect:

  • ক) Systolic BP < 90 mmHg: Indicates shock or severe dehydration, but is not the specific biochemical marker of severe ketoacidosis.

  • গ) Anion gap > 8 mmol/L: An elevated anion gap indicates metabolic acidosis, but mild elevation can occur; severe DKA usually has a much higher anion gap.

  • ঘ) Bicarbonate < 16 mmol/L: Suggests metabolic acidosis but is usually associated with moderate DKA; severe DKA typically has bicarbonate <10 mmol/L.

High-Yield Rapid Recall

  • DKA severity criteria (commonly used):

    • Mild: Glucose >250 mg/dL, pH 7.25–7.30, bicarbonate 15–18 mmol/L.

    • Moderate: pH 7.00–7.24, bicarbonate 10–15 mmol/L.

    • Severe: pH <7.00, bicarbonate <10 mmol/L, blood ketones >6 mmol/L.

  • DKA triad: Hyperglycemia + Ketosis + Metabolic acidosis.

  • Anion gap: Increased due to accumulation of ketoacids.

  • Treatment: IV fluids + insulin + potassium monitoring.

  • Common MCQ trap: Ketone level >6 mmol/L = severe DKA marker.

Exam Pearl

In DKA, remember: Blood ketones >6 mmol/L indicates severe ketoacidosis.
